titleEn: Gezelligheid: why Dutch plans are judged by how the room feels
facts: Gezelligheid is an untranslatable Dutch noun for a shared atmosphere of warmth and belonging, used about homes, cafés, offices and even train compartments.
The word works as an adjective (gezellig) and as a verdict: an evening can be gezellig or fail to be, and hosts plan lighting, seating and snacks around it.
It is bound up with the Dutch habit of gathering at home rather than in restaurants, over coffee or beer and a modest round of biscuits.
Dutch social life often runs on appointments; an unexpected visit can be less gezellig because it interrupts the household's schedule.
The concept marks belonging: a space becomes gezellig when everyone is included, so exclusion is felt as a physical chill.
exampleEn: A Dutch colleague invites you for koffie om vier uur; the visit lasts the hour it was planned for, with one biscuit, and both host and guest call it gezellig.
qualificationEn: Gezelligheid is a cultural keyword, not a claim that all Dutch homes are cosy; students, renters and immigrant households use the word with different resources and meanings.

titleEn: Janteloven: the Nordic code that polices success
facts: The Law of Jante comes from Aksel Sandemose's 1933 satirical novel A Fugitive Crosses His Tracks, set in the fictional Danish town of Jante.
Its ten rules include 'You shall not think you are special' and 'You shall not think you are as good as us'.
Sandemose described a small-town conformity that punished ambition; Scandinavians later adopted janteloven as shorthand for exactly that pressure.
The code is invoked in debates about entrepreneurship, school grading and celebrity, and defenders say it protects equality while critics say it stifles excellence.
It is neither law nor uniquely Nordic, but the term is so widely used that Nordic politicians and business leaders regularly complain about it.
exampleEn: A Danish start-up founder is congratulated but also teased for 'believing you are something', a reaction colleagues may call janteloven.
qualificationEn: Janteloven is a satirical literary invention used as a cultural lens; it is not a behavioural rulebook, and urban, younger and immigrant Scandinavians relate to it very differently.

titleEn: Fika: the Swedish coffee break that is really a social obligation
facts: Fika is a Swedish coffee break, usually with something sweet, taken mid-morning and mid-afternoon at workplaces and in homes.
Sweden ranks among the world's top coffee consumers per capita, and fika is both noun and verb: you fika, and you are invited to fika.
The classic pairing is coffee with a cinnamon bun (kanelbulle), but the point is the pause and the company rather than the drink.
Many Swedish workplaces treat the shared fika as part of the working day, and skipping it repeatedly can read as opting out of the team.
Fika has spread abroad as a café concept, but in Sweden it is cheap, ordinary and frequent rather than a special treat.
exampleEn: At 14:30 a Swedish office empties into the kitchen, the coffee is already on, someone has brought buns, and the meeting stops for twenty minutes.
qualificationEn: Fika frequency and form vary by workplace, generation and region; in some offices it is sacrosanct, in others it has shrunk to a quick coffee, and remote work has changed it.

titleEn: Dugnad: the Norwegian weekend when the whole block works
facts: Dugnad is organised voluntary work for a shared benefit, traditionally in housing cooperatives, sports clubs, schools and neighbourhoods.
Norwegian housing cooperatives (borettslag) often schedule dugnads to paint, rake, clean or repair shared areas.
The work is unpaid but socially binding: residents are expected to turn up, and lists and coffee breaks make participation visible.
The word also covers fundraising drives and club work; sports clubs rely on parents' dugnad shifts for everything from canteen duty to track maintenance.
As paid services and long commutes spread, some cooperatives struggle to fill their dugnad lists, and a few now fine absent households.
exampleEn: On a Saturday in May, residents of an Oslo block gather at 10:00 to rake the courtyard, share waffles at noon, and finish by early afternoon.
qualificationEn: Dugnad is an ideal as much as a practice; participation varies by neighbourhood, age and income, and newcomers may need time to learn the unwritten expectations.

titleEn: In Finland the sauna is a room for talking, not just sweating
facts: Finland has roughly three million saunas for a population of about 5.6 million, in homes, apartment blocks, lakeside cottages and public halls.
Finnish sauna culture was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in December 2020.
A sauna session is social and unhurried: löyly (steam from water thrown on the stones), cooling outside, and conversation in the heat.
Nudity is ordinary inside the sauna, but behaviour is carefully governed: no staring, and public sessions are usually segregated unless advertised otherwise.
The sauna is also a diplomatic and business setting; Finnish hosts may invite guests to sauna because it is seen as a levelling, trusting space.
exampleEn: A Finnish family heats the cottage sauna on Saturday evening, goes in and out to the lake, and eats afterwards without anyone treating the nudity as remarkable.
qualificationEn: Sauna habits vary between families, regions and public institutions; not every Finn likes saunas, and immigrant and younger urban Finns may use them less.

titleEn: Allotments: the British shed-and-vegetable society behind the hedge
facts: An allotment is a plot rented from a council, parish or private landlord for growing food, usually with a shed, water butt and rules about hedges and bonfires.
Allotments became widespread in 19th-century industrial towns and were protected by the 1908 Small Holdings and Allotments Act, which obliged councils to provide land.
Plots are typically measured in rods or poles (about 250 square metres for ten rods), and waiting lists in cities can run for years.
The culture is as much social as horticultural: site committees, seed swaps, shared tools, gossip over the fence and competitions for the best onion.
Allotmenteering has revived among younger growers and food enthusiasts, while developers and councils argue over the value of urban land.
exampleEn: On a Sunday morning an allotment site fills with people in wellies; one plot holder puts the kettle on in a shed while another trades tomato seedlings over the fence.
qualificationEn: Allotment law and waiting lists differ across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and not every site is sociable; some are solitary and rule-bound.

titleEn: The craic: how Irish social life turns talk into a shared event
facts: Craic (also crack) means news, gossip, fun and enjoyable conversation, and 'What's the craic?' can mean 'How are you?' or 'What's happening?'.
The word was borrowed from Scots and English crack into Irish in the mid-20th century, and the Irish spelling was then reborrowed into English.
Having the craic describes a good time that depends on wit and company rather than money or a venue.
In pubs the term sets expectations: conversation is the entertainment, and a quiet room can still be a great night if the talk is good.
The phrase has become an Irish export used in tourism and diaspora marketing, which some Irish people find overstated.
exampleEn: Two friends meet for one pint, stay three hours because the craic is good, and the evening is judged a success even though nothing was planned.
qualificationEn: Craic is a word and an ideal, not a guarantee; Irish social life ranges from quiet rural visits to noisy city nights, and the term is used self-consciously as well as sincerely.

titleEn: La bise: counting kisses correctly in France
facts: La bise is a cheek-to-cheek greeting, usually two kisses in Paris and much of northern France, three in parts of the south and west, and four in some Breton villages.
The greeting is common between friends, relatives and colleagues, but not in formal business meetings, where a handshake is safer.
The mechanics are quick and airy: cheeks touch lightly, and the number of kisses is regional knowledge that even French people can get wrong when they move.
During the pandemic la bise became a public-health issue and was temporarily discouraged, showing how routine the gesture is.
Schoolchildren learn the local count, and adults often ask 'on se fait la bise ?' before leaning in.
exampleEn: At a family lunch in Lyon a late guest makes the rounds, three kisses per adult, while a colleague visiting from Paris is surprised to receive four in Brittany.
qualificationEn: The number of kisses and who participates vary sharply by region, generation and setting; la bise is not universal in France, and many people avoid it at work or with strangers.

titleEn: Tu or vous: the French pronoun that negotiates the relationship
facts: French has two singular 'you' pronouns: tu for closeness and vous for formality, distance or plural address.
Adults usually start with vous and move to tu only when one side proposes it, often with 'on se tutoie ?'.
The choice is not just politeness: it encodes age, hierarchy, intimacy and whether a relationship has changed.
Workplaces vary: some teams tutoie from day one, others keep vous with senior colleagues for years; families usually use tu, but some grandparents receive vous.
Getting it wrong can cause real awkwardness, and French people often negotiate the switch explicitly.
exampleEn: A new employee calls her manager vous for months; after a team lunch he says 'on se tutoie', and she switches mid-sentence, slightly relieved.
qualificationEn: Usage differs by region, generation, workplace and family; Quebec French and some African varieties have their own conventions, and younger speakers increasingly tutoie more freely.

expression.glossEn: Can we use tu with each other?

titleEn: Sobremesa: the Spanish meal that continues after the plates
facts: Sobremesa literally means 'over the table': the time spent talking after a meal, with coffee, a small liqueur or nothing at all.
It is a recognised social institution in Spain, where lunch is often the main meal and can last into the late afternoon.
The conversation is the point; restaurants may turn tables, but a family home expects guests to stay and talk.
The habit is tied to a slower meal culture and to the separation of lunch from the working day, though city schedules are tightening.
Sobremesa is also used for business and political talk, and many deals are said to be settled after the coffee arrives.
exampleEn: A Sunday lunch in Valencia finishes at four, but the family stays at the table until six, moving from coffee to a bottle of orujo and unfinished arguments about football.
qualificationEn: Sobremesa is strongest at family meals and in smaller towns; in big-city offices lunch may be a sandwich, and younger Spaniards often report less time for it.

titleEn: The siesta is shorter, rarer and more practical than the postcard
facts: The siesta is a short early-afternoon nap, traditionally after the midday meal and in the hottest part of the day.
In Spain the long lunch-and-sleep break is mostly a rural and small-town habit, and many Spaniards in cities do not nap at all.
The Spanish working day is famously long, with a break that can include lunch and a rest, pushing the evening meal late.
Some towns still close shops for a midday pause, especially in summer, but retail hours and commuting have eroded the practice.
The word has become a tourist cliche that annoys Spaniards who work through the afternoon.
exampleEn: In a small Andalusian town in August the streets empty after 14:00, shutters come down, and the post office reopens at 17:00; in Madrid the same afternoon is a normal workday.
qualificationEn: Siesta habits vary enormously by region, season and job; the tourist image of an entire nation asleep is inaccurate, and many Spaniards defend the break as a sensible response to heat.

titleEn: Saudade: the Portuguese word for a longing that has no cure
facts: Saudade is a Portuguese noun for a melancholic, nostalgic longing for someone or something absent, often with the sense that it may never return.
It derives from the Latin word for solitude and appears in Portuguese and Galician literature, fado lyrics and everyday speech.
The word can be used lightly ('que saudade!' when a favourite food reappears) or deeply, and that ambiguity is part of its cultural weight.
Brazilian Portuguese uses it constantly, and the concept travelled with Portuguese migration into diaspora communities.
There is no single English equivalent; translations such as longing or missing lose the acceptance of absence.
exampleEn: A Lisbon grandmother tastes her mother's rice pudding and says 'que saudade', meaning both the pleasure of remembering and the pain of the loss.
qualificationEn: Saudade is a keyword, not a national temperament; Portuguese and Brazilian speakers use it with irony, exaggeration and everyday lightness, and the sad-nation reading is a literary cliche.

expression.glossEn: a bittersweet longing for an absent person, place or time

titleEn: How to drink coffee standing up in Italy
facts: Italians drink espresso at the bar, standing, often in a few minutes, and the price is usually lower al banco than at a table.
Coffee is a morning and after-meal ritual: cappuccino is typically a breakfast drink, while espresso follows lunch or dinner.
The barista is addressed by title and order ('un caffè, per favore'), and the coffee is drunk quickly at the counter.
In Naples and other southern cities the caffè sospeso, a coffee paid forward for a stranger, is a well-known local custom.
Home espresso pots (moka) and office coffee machines coexist with the bar, so the bar is social as much as caffèinated.
exampleEn: At 07:45 a Milanese bar is full of people standing at the counter; a man orders un caffè, drinks it in two sips, leaves a coin and is at his desk by 08:00.
qualificationEn: Habits differ between north and south, city and village; not every Italian drinks espresso daily, and the no-cappuccino-after-lunch rule is a strong convention rather than a law.

titleEn: Philotimo: the Greek value that rewards doing right quietly
facts: Philotimo literally means love of honour but describes a cluster of virtues: self-respect, generosity, courage and doing the right thing without being asked.
It is invoked as praise for someone who helps a stranger, keeps a promise or refuses to shame their family.
The concept is relational: it depends on how one's actions are seen by family and community, and it can require hospitality beyond one's means.
It is taught informally through family example and church, and Greek schools and public discourse still use it as a national ideal.
Philotimo can also have a defensive side: a slight to honour may demand a response, which is why the term is debated as both virtue and burden.
exampleEn: A Greek shopkeeper refuses payment for a small repair and says it is philotimo, meaning he would be ashamed to charge a neighbour for that.
qualificationEn: Philotimo is an ideal, not a description of every Greek; its meaning shifts between generations and between rural and urban settings, and it can justify both generosity and stubborn pride.

titleEn: Imieniny: why Poles celebrate a name more than a birthday
facts: Imieniny is the celebration of one's name day, the feast of the patron saint after whom a person is named, marked in the Polish calendar.
Traditionally name days had greater social weight than birthdays, and in many families they still involve flowers, gifts, cake and visits.
Workplaces mark them too: colleagues bring flowers and sweets, and a name day can be a bigger office event than a birthday.
The date depends on the saint's day, so people with the same first name celebrate together, and calendars print the names for each day.
Birthdays are now more popular among younger Poles, but name days remain strong in older generations and in the countryside.
exampleEn: On 24 June, everyone named Jan in a Polish office gets a bunch of flowers and a box of chocolates, and the coffee room fills with good wishes.
qualificationEn: Not every Pole celebrates name days, and the custom varies by region, family tradition and generation; some names have several possible dates, and many younger people barely notice theirs.

titleEn: Dacha life: the Russian country house as family and neighbour network
facts: A dacha is a seasonal or year-round second home outside the city, often with a garden plot and a small house.
Dachas date from the tsarist era but became mass phenomena in the Soviet period, when families were allotted land and built simple cottages.
The dacha is a family project: grandparents garden, parents repair, children are sent for the summer, and neighbours share tools and produce.
The garden is not just leisure: many families grow potatoes, cucumbers, berries and preserves that carry them through winter.
The banya, a shed and a samovar are common features, and weekend dacha trains are a recognisable part of Russian city life.
exampleEn: On Friday evening a Moscow family drives two hours to its dacha, spends Saturday weeding and repairing the fence, and returns on Sunday with jars of pickles for the winter.
qualificationEn: Dacha culture varies by region, income and generation; younger urban Russians may inherit dachas without gardening them, and many families have no dacha at all.

titleEn: Slava: the Serbian family feast that belongs to a saint
facts: Slava is a Serbian Orthodox family celebration of the household's patron saint, passed down patrilineally through generations.
The family invites guests, lights candles, cuts a special bread (kolač) and serves food; the saint's day is fixed by the Orthodox calendar.
The custom blends church ritual with family hospitality, and the host is expected to welcome anyone who comes, including unexpected visitors.
Different families celebrate different saints, so Slava dates are spread across the year and can be a public as well as private event.
The tradition is also kept by Serbian communities abroad, where it becomes a marker of identity.
exampleEn: On a Slava day in Belgrade a family's door stays busy from morning; guests bring wine and sweets, and the host serves the same feast to relatives, neighbours and a passing friend.
qualificationEn: Practice varies between urban and rural families, and some younger Serbs treat Slava as a family gathering more than a religious observance; other Orthodox Balkan peoples have related but distinct customs.

titleEn: Çay: Turkey's tea glass as an instrument of hospitality
facts: Turkey has the world's highest per-capita tea consumption, over 3 kilograms per person a year.
Çay is brewed in a double pot (çaydanlık), strong in the top and diluted with hot water from the bottom, and served in a small tulip-shaped glass.
Offering tea is a basic gesture of welcome; refusing it is possible, but accepting starts a small social exchange.
Tea houses (çay bahçesi or kahvehane) are male-dominated social spaces in many towns, while tea is served everywhere from shops to barbers.
The tea is usually taken with sugar cubes and without milk, and a glass is often refilled until the guest signals enough.
exampleEn: A carpet seller in Istanbul orders two glasses of çay for a browsing customer, and the conversation starts before any price is discussed.
qualificationEn: Tea habits vary by region, generation and setting; younger urban Turks drink more coffee and herbal teas, and the refill-until-you-refuse expectation is stronger in some regions than others.

titleEn: The Viennese coffee house: a living room with waiters
facts: The Viennese coffee house is a distinct institution where guests can sit for hours over a single coffee, reading newspapers on wooden holders.
Since 2011 the Viennese coffee house culture has been listed in Austria's national inventory of intangible cultural heritage.
Classic orders include the Melange (coffee with milk), Einspanner (with whipped cream) and a glass of water served automatically with the coffee.
Waiters in traditional houses are famously formal, and the café is a place for newspapers, conversation, chess and solitary work.
The coffee house historically hosted writers, politicians and revolutionaries, and it still functions as a semi-public living room.
exampleEn: A Viennese pensioner orders a Melange, unfolds three newspapers on their holders, and stays until lunch without being asked to leave.
qualificationEn: Traditional coffee houses coexist with modern cafés and chains; younger Austrians may use them differently, and the sit-all-day norm is stronger in the historic houses than everywhere.

titleEn: The Stammtisch: Germany's reserved table and its social order
facts: A Stammtisch is a regulars' table: an informal group that meets at the same pub or restaurant on a fixed evening.
The table itself is often marked with a sign or plaque reserving it, and the group may have an informal hierarchy of seniority.
Stammtische exist for sports clubs, card games, work colleagues and village associations, and they function as low-cost social membership.
The term also carries a political meaning: Stammtischpolitik describes loud, simplified opinions expressed among regulars.
Newcomers are usually introduced by a member rather than simply sitting down, because the table is a social boundary.
exampleEn: Every Thursday at 19:00 the same eight men occupy a corner table in a Swabian pub, a brass sign names the club, and a newcomer waits to be invited before sitting.
qualificationEn: The Stammtisch is in decline in some cities as pubs close and schedules fragment, and it is not a universal German institution; clubs, cafés and kitchens host similar gatherings differently.

titleEn: Jólabókaflóð: Iceland's Christmas book flood
facts: Jólabókaflóð means Christmas book flood: the annual autumn release of new books in Iceland ahead of the gift-giving season.
Publishers issue a free catalogue, Bókatíðindi, distributed to households in November so people can choose books as presents.
Books are the most popular Christmas gift in Iceland, and many families exchange them on Christmas Eve and spend the evening reading.
The tradition is linked to the post-war period, when paper was relatively available and books were a practical gift in a small economy.
It has become an exportable image of Icelandic cosiness, but it remains a real publishing season on which authors and shops depend.
exampleEn: An Icelandic family opens presents on Christmas Eve, and each person disappears to a sofa with a new book and a box of chocolate.
qualificationEn: The reading-and-chocolate part is a popular ideal rather than a universal ritual; gift habits, budgets and family customs vary, and the book flood is above all a publishing phenomenon.

titleEn: In Hungarian, the family name comes first
facts: Hungarian names are normally written and spoken with the family name first, then the given name: Kovács János, not János Kovács.
This eastern name order is standard in Hungarian, and the same order is used in official documents, school lists and phone books.
When Hungarians write in English or German they often reverse the order, which can cause confusion at borders and in academic citations.
The order reflects a wider pattern: dates are written year-month-day, and addresses run from larger to smaller unit.
Foreign names are usually kept in their original order, so a Hungarian sentence may mix two naming systems.
exampleEn: A Hungarian student in Berlin fills in a form and has to decide whether Kovács is the first name or the surname; in Budapest the same order is obvious.
qualificationEn: The order is consistent in Hungarian, but Hungarians adapt it when writing in other languages, and foreign residents may use Western order even in Hungarian contexts.

expression.glossEn: family name first, given name second - the standard Hungarian order

titleEn: Nomikai: the Japanese after-work party that is work
facts: A nomikai is a drinking party organised by a workplace, school club or friendship group, usually held in an izakaya or restaurant.
The group sits at one long table, starts with a toast (kanpai), and often pays a fixed course price including all-you-can-drink (nomihodai).
A kanji (organiser) handles the booking and collection, and juniors often pour for seniors while seating follows rank.
Attendance can feel obligatory even when unpaid, and the second party (nijikai) may move to a bar or karaoke.
Remote work and younger employees' preferences have weakened the institution, but it remains a common way to build workplace ties.
exampleEn: A Tokyo team of twelve takes a reserved izakaya room at 19:00, toasts, and a junior member walks around pouring beer for senior colleagues before eating.
qualificationEn: Not every Japanese worker attends or enjoys nomikai; company culture, age and region matter, and many firms have cut back on obligatory drinking since the 2010s.

titleEn: The genkan: where Japanese homes decide who comes in
facts: The genkan is the entryway inside a Japanese home where shoes are removed before stepping up into the main floor.
It is a physical and social threshold: the shoe-removal point marks the boundary between outside and inside, and guests are expected to turn their shoes to face the door.
Homes usually provide slippers for guests, and separate slippers are kept for the toilet; tatami rooms may require bare or socked feet.
The genkan also receives deliveries and is where umbrellas, keys and school bags are left, making it a small daily staging area.
Business visitors and delivery staff often stay at the genkan and do not enter the house, which keeps the home's inner space protected.
exampleEn: A visitor steps into a narrow genkan, takes off their shoes, turns them around, puts on the guest slippers offered, and only then is invited into the living room.
qualificationEn: Genkan design varies between houses, apartments and regions; some modern homes have small entries, and Western-style housing in Japan may not follow the same shoe rules.

titleEn: Nunchi: reading the room as a Korean social skill
facts: Nunchi (눈치) is the Korean idea of sensing other people's moods and the atmosphere of a situation before anything is said.
The word combines eye and measure, and it is treated as a skill that children learn at home and adults are judged on.
High nunchi means knowing when to speak, when to leave, and what a host actually wants; low nunchi is a common criticism.
It matters in hierarchy: junior people are expected to notice when a senior needs something, and silence can carry a message.
The concept overlaps with emotional intelligence but is more relational and status-aware, and it shapes workplace and family interaction.
exampleEn: At a Korean dinner a guest notices the host glancing at the clock, reads the nunchi, and says goodbye before being asked to leave.
qualificationEn: Nunchi is an ideal, and Koreans vary in how much they value or perform it; younger people sometimes push back against the indirectness it encourages, and the concept is not a fixed national trait.

expression.glossEn: the ability to read a room and gauge others' moods without being told

titleEn: Guanxi: how relationships do work in Chinese society
facts: Guanxi describes a personal network of relationships through which favours, information and opportunities flow, based on mutual obligation.
It is built through repeated contact, gift-giving, meals and help with problems, and it carries an expectation of reciprocity (renqing).
Guanxi matters in business, hiring, healthcare and schooling, where personal connections can supplement formal procedures.
It is not simply corruption: many Chinese distinguish ordinary relationship-building from illegal bribery, though the line is debated.
Urbanisation and digital platforms have changed how networks form, but family and native-place ties remain central.
exampleEn: A Shanghai entrepreneur asks a former classmate to introduce them to a factory manager, then returns the favour months later by helping the classmate's nephew find an internship.
qualificationEn: Guanxi is not a single system and its importance varies by sector, region and generation; formal rules have tightened, and many Chinese resent being expected to rely on connections.

titleEn: Guangchangwu: China's public-square dancing and the fight over shared space
facts: Guangchangwu (public square dance) is a mass exercise-and-dance routine performed to loud music in parks and plazas, mostly by middle-aged and retired women.
Groups form around a leader with a portable speaker, learn set routines, and dance in the morning or evening.
The activity is social: it gives retirees exercise, company and a visible place in the city, often after children have left home.
It has caused noise disputes with nearby residents, leading some cities to restrict hours, volume or locations.
The government has both promoted it as healthy mass culture and tried to regulate it, and it has become a symbol of China's ageing society.
exampleEn: At 19:30 a square in Chengdu fills with dozens of women in matching jackets, a speaker is placed on a bench, and the same routine begins for the third time that week.
qualificationEn: Participation is concentrated among older women in cities; not all Chinese approve of it, and noise conflicts have made it controversial in dense neighbourhoods.

titleEn: Namaste: the greeting that puts the hands before the words
facts: Namaste is a greeting used across Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions, spoken with palms pressed together and a slight bow.
The gesture is called añjali mudrā; the word means roughly 'I bow to you', and it can be used at any time of day.
It works across age and status because it does not require touching, which also makes it convenient in hot weather and between strangers.
Indians often say namaste with a folded-hands gesture when meeting, parting, thanking or praying, and the gesture alone can carry the greeting.
In the diaspora and global yoga culture the word has become a generic hello, which some Indians find flattened.
exampleEn: A Delhi shopkeeper greets a customer with a small bow and pressed palms, and the customer returns the gesture before asking for prices.
qualificationEn: Greetings vary by region, religion and setting; namaste is common but not universal in India, and younger urban Indians may use hi or a handshake with equals.

expression.glossEn: I bow to you - hello, used with palms together

titleEn: The Indian head bobble is not a yes or a no
facts: The head bobble is a side-to-side roll of the head, common in South Asia and especially India, used as nonverbal communication.
Its meaning depends on context: it can signal yes, maybe, okay, I understand, or simply that the person is listening.
Foreign visitors often read it as a no or as indecision, which can lead to misunderstanding in shops, offices and negotiations.
The gesture is not formal etiquette but a habit picked up socially, and many Indians are unaware they are doing it.
It is one of several nonverbal cues, along with hand gestures, eyebrow movement and silence, that carry meaning in Indian conversation.
exampleEn: A visitor asks an Indian colleague whether the report is finished; the colleague tilts their head from side to side while saying 'yes, almost', and the visitor is unsure how to take it.
qualificationEn: Not all Indians bobble, and the gesture's meaning is highly contextual; region, language and individual habit matter, so it should be read alongside words and tone.

titleEn: Adda: the Bengali art of doing nothing together
facts: Adda is a Bengali term for unhurried informal socialising, typically in neighbourhoods, homes, tea stalls, clubs and parks.
It is not a planned meeting so much as a culture of hanging out, where conversation ranges from politics and literature to gossip and jokes.
The activity was historically associated with educated urban men but has become more heterogeneous, including women and students.
Adda entered the Oxford English Dictionary in 2004, reflecting its recognition as a distinct cultural practice.
In Dhaka and Kolkata, adda often happens over tea and snacks, and it can last for hours without a fixed purpose.
exampleEn: On a Friday evening in Dhaka, four friends meet at a tea stall with no plan, order cha, and stay three hours arguing about cricket and poetry.
qualificationEn: Adda is a Bengali cultural ideal rather than a universal practice; class, gender, generation and city shape who can take part and where, and busy work schedules have narrowed it for some.

expression.glossEn: an unhurried hangout with talk, tea and no fixed agenda

titleEn: Gotong royong: Indonesia's mutual-aid habit and its modern limits
facts: Gotong royong means mutual assistance: neighbours work together on shared tasks such as cleaning drains, building a mosque, or repairing a village road.
The principle is rooted in village life and was later adopted as a national slogan by the Indonesian state.
It is organised through neighbourhood associations (RT/RW) and often announced by a drum or loudspeaker.
Work is unpaid and social: food is shared, absentees may be noted, and the event reinforces who belongs to the community.
In large cities, commuting and apartment living have weakened the practice, though it revives around disasters and communal events.
exampleEn: On a Sunday morning in a Jakarta kampung, residents sweep the lane and clear the drainage channel together, then share rice and coffee at the end.
qualificationEn: Gotong royong is an ideal as well as a practice; participation varies by neighbourhood and class, and the term has been used politically, so not every Indonesian experiences it as voluntary.

titleEn: Bayanihan: the Filipino idea of moving a house together
facts: Bayanihan describes communal cooperation, traditionally illustrated by neighbours carrying a house on poles to a new site.
The word comes from bayan, meaning town or community, and the practice is associated with rural barangay life.
It appears today in volunteer brigades, disaster relief, school clean-ups and neighbourhood projects.
The image of the moving house is iconic but largely historical; the value survives more than the practice.
Bayanihan is taught in schools as a national virtue and invoked by politicians, which makes it both a genuine norm and a rhetorical tool.
exampleEn: After a typhoon, a barangay organises a bayanihan crew to clear a fallen tree from the road before government help arrives.
qualificationEn: Bayanihan is an ideal that can be romanticised; urban Filipinos may rarely experience it, and the term can obscure the real labour and unequal burdens behind community projects.

titleEn: The wai: Thailand's greeting as a small statement of rank
facts: The wai is a greeting made by pressing the palms together in a prayer-like gesture with a slight bow.
The height of the hands and depth of the bow signal respect: hands near the chest for peers, higher and deeper for elders, monks or teachers.
The greeting has Indian origins and is related to namaste, and it is used for hello, goodbye, thanks and apology.
Thais usually return a wai, but juniors initiate it and seniors may acknowledge with a nod rather than a full wai.
The gesture is common but not universal; handshakes are used in business with foreigners, and the wai has become a symbol of Thai identity.
exampleEn: A student greets a teacher with a wai, hands raised near the face, while the teacher replies with a smaller wai and a nod.
qualificationEn: Wai etiquette varies by region and setting; not every Thai wais every time, and the gesture's meaning can shift with age, status and the presence of foreigners.

expression.glossEn: hello - usually said while making the wai gesture

titleEn: Vietnamese pronouns: every you is a family role
facts: Vietnamese pronouns are largely kinship terms: speakers choose words like anh (older brother), chị (older sister), em (younger sibling) or ông/bà (grandfather/grandmother) for you and I.
The choice depends on age, gender, status and relationship, so pronouns can change as a friendship or a career develops.
Using the wrong term can sound presumptuous or cold, and speakers often adjust after learning someone's age.
The system is flexible: em can address a younger stranger, a romantic partner or a waiter, with tone and context doing the rest.
In formal or public settings Vietnamese may use tôi and bạn, but kinship terms remain the everyday default.
exampleEn: A Hanoi student calls a slightly older colleague anh and refers to herself as em; when she later becomes his manager, the pronouns become awkward and they negotiate new ones.
qualificationEn: Usage varies by region, generation and setting, and diaspora Vietnamese may mix patterns; the kinship system is a resource, not a rigid rulebook, and speakers bend it constantly.

expression.glossEn: older-brother plus calling particle: a warm way to call a man slightly older than you

titleEn: Mamak stalls: Malaysia's 24-hour social kitchens
facts: Mamak stalls are open-air or indoor eateries run mostly by Tamil Muslims, found across Malaysia and Singapore.
They serve roti canai, teh tarik, mee goreng and other halal food, often late into the night or around the clock.
The stall is a social institution: people gather over tea, watch football, argue politics and linger without being rushed.
Teh tarik (pulled tea) is made by pouring the drink between two cups, and the theatre of preparation is part of the appeal.
Mamak culture cuts across ethnicity, class and religion, making it one of the few shared public spaces in a segmented society.
exampleEn: At 1 a.m. in Kuala Lumpur a mamak stall is full: a group of students shares roti canai, an uncle nurses a teh tarik, and football plays on a wall-mounted television.
qualificationEn: Mamak stalls are not the only Malaysian eating culture, and their clientele varies by neighbourhood; gentrification, licensing and labour issues are changing the traditional all-night model.

titleEn: Kiasu: Singapore's fear of losing and the queue it creates
facts: Kiasu comes from Hokkien kia (afraid) and su (to lose), and describes the fear of missing out or losing out.
In Singapore it is used affectionately and critically: queueing early, grabbing freebies, booking the best seat, or stocking up before a shortage.
The term entered Singlish in the 1980s and has become a national shorthand for competitive caution.
It is linked to Singapore's high-stakes education and housing systems, where small advantages can matter.
The government has periodically campaigned against kiasu behaviour while also relying on competitive instincts for economic success.
exampleEn: A shopper joins a queue that has formed outside a new bakery without knowing what is being sold, a joke Singaporeans tell about kiasu.
qualificationEn: Kiasu is a label people apply to themselves and others; it is not a description of every Singaporean, and the behaviour can be a rational response to scarce housing, school places and limited land.

titleEn: Inside the ger: Mongolian hospitality and the rules of the round house
facts: The Mongolian ger (often called a yurt) is a round, felt-covered tent with a wooden lattice frame, still home to many herding families and common in Ulaanbaatar's ger districts.
Its layout is ordered: the door faces south, the hearth is central, the north side is for honoured guests, and the west side is traditionally for men while the east is for women and cooking.
Guests are expected to enter without stepping on the threshold, move clockwise, and accept offered milk tea or dairy products.
Hospitality is practical in a sparse landscape: herders offer shelter and food to travellers, and refusing too firmly can seem rude.
The ger is also a national symbol, used in festivals and tourism, even as most Mongolians now live in apartments.
exampleEn: A herder family welcomes a traveller into their ger, pours milk tea, and offers a bowl of dried curd while gesturing to the north side for the guest to sit.
qualificationEn: Ger etiquette varies between families, regions and urban settings; young Mongolians may keep only some rules, and the yurt of tourism is not the same as a working herding home.

titleEn: Dastarkhan: the Kazakh table that must never look empty
facts: Dastarkhan is the Central Asian term for the spread tablecloth, and by extension the hospitality and abundance of a meal.
In Kazakhstan a guest is offered tea, baursak (fried dough), dried fruit and sweets before anything else, and the table is expected to be generous.
Meat dishes carry status: beshbarmak (meat with noodles) is served for important guests, and the host may allocate particular cuts according to age and rank.
Tea is poured continuously, and a guest who has had enough can cover the cup or refuse with a word.
The dastarkhan is central to weddings, funerals and family gatherings, where the size of the spread reflects the host's standing.
exampleEn: A Kazakh family receives a guest with tea and baursak, then a plate of beshbarmak; the host places the sheep's head before the most honoured person at the table.
qualificationEn: Dastarkhan customs differ between Kazakh, Uzbek and other Central Asian traditions; urban families may simplify the meal, and the never-empty-table ideal can be a financial burden.

titleEn: Mahalla: the Uzbek neighbourhood that governs everyday life
facts: A mahalla is a traditional neighbourhood community in Uzbekistan and other parts of Central Asia, with its own elders, meeting place and informal authority.
Mahalla committees help organise weddings, funerals, charity, street cleaning and dispute mediation.
The institution was formalised under Soviet rule and has continued under independence, making it both a state-linked body and a community network.
Neighbours are expected to attend each other's life-cycle events, and contributions, financial or in labour, are pooled.
Mahalla identity remains strong in old city quarters, even as apartment living and migration change neighbourhood life.
exampleEn: When a family in a Tashkent mahalla holds a wedding, neighbours help cook, lend dishes and organise the courtyard seating, while the mahalla committee keeps the peace.
qualificationEn: Mahalla life is stronger in some regions and old quarters than others; urban apartment dwellers may barely know theirs, and the institution has been criticised for social pressure and surveillance.

titleEn: The tamada: Georgia's toastmaster runs the table
facts: A tamada is the toastmaster at a Georgian supra (feast), responsible for introducing each toast and keeping the table's rhythm.
Every supra, large or small, has a tamada; Georgians say the tamada is dictator of the table.
The role requires wit, memory and diplomacy: the tamada decides who speaks, when to eat, and how the evening moves.
Toasts are elaborate and ordered, covering family, friends, the dead, peace and guests, and guests are expected to respond.
The tamada also regulates drinking, often calling on others to drain their glasses while managing the pace.
exampleEn: At a Tbilisi birthday supra the tamada rises for each toast, names the person being honoured, and signals when everyone should drink, while the table waits for his cue.
qualificationEn: Supra style varies by region, family and occasion; younger Georgians may run looser gatherings, and the tamada's authority is playful as well as real.

titleEn: Taarof: the Iranian etiquette of refusing what you want
facts: Taarof is an Iranian system of ritual politeness that governs offers, refusals and deference in everyday interaction.
A shopkeeper may refuse payment, a host may insist a guest stay for dinner, and a guest may decline several times before accepting.
The ritual is not simply insincere: it establishes respect and relative rank while giving both sides room to negotiate.
Taarof has a linguistic side, with formulaic phrases and elaborate courtesies, and a behavioural side, such as letting others pass first.
Iranians often signal when taarof is not expected, for example by saying taarof nakonid (don't taarof), to move to plain speech.
exampleEn: At a Tehran fruit stall the seller says ghabeli nadare (it is not worth your paying), the customer insists on paying, and both know the ritual ends with money changing hands.
qualificationEn: Taarof is a cultural grammar, not a fixed script; younger Iranians, diaspora communities and formal settings use it in different doses, and foreigners can mistake ritual refusal for a real one.

expression.glossEn: I am your sacrifice - a courtesy meaning you first or after you

titleEn: Dugri: the Israeli preference for straight talk
facts: Dugri (from Arabic straight) is Israeli slang for direct, unadorned speech: saying what you mean without softening it.
The style is associated with the sabra, the native-born Israeli stereotype of a prickly exterior and warm interior.
Dugri is valued as honest and efficient in workplaces, army units and casual friendships, where indirectness can be read as evasive.
It can also wound: newcomers and visitors may experience the same directness as bluntness or rudeness.
The term is used self-consciously, and Israelis often distinguish dugri from simply being aggressive.
exampleEn: An Israeli colleague tells a new hire 'your presentation was weak' in the corridor, then helps them rewrite it, expecting no offence to be taken.
qualificationEn: Israeli communication varies by community, generation and setting; religious, Arab and immigrant Israelis may use different norms, and dugri is a stereotype as much as a practice.

expression.glossEn: straight talk; saying it as it is

titleEn: The majlis: the Gulf's room for guests and decisions
facts: A majlis is a sitting room and a gathering: a space in the home or a dedicated hall where guests are received and matters are discussed.
In Gulf societies the majlis traditionally hosts relatives, neighbours and visitors, with seating arranged by age and status and coffee served soon after arrival.
The institution also has a public dimension: majlis-style meetings connect rulers, tribes and communities, and the word is used for councils and legislatures.
Hospitality is formalised: the host greets guests, offers dates and cardamom coffee, and conversation may range from family news to business.
In the UAE, majlis culture is promoted as heritage, and new forms such as youth majlis and women's majlis have appeared.
exampleEn: In an Abu Dhabi home, male guests are shown into the majlis, served Arabic coffee from a dallah, and sit in a circle while the host asks about their families.
qualificationEn: Majlis customs differ across the Gulf and between households; gender-separated gatherings are common but not universal, and urban life has changed the frequency and form of the institution.

sources.title: Culture of the United Arab Emirates

titleEn: Café Touba: Senegal's spiced coffee of the street
facts: Café Touba is a Senegalese coffee flavoured with djar (grains of Selim) and sometimes cloves, named after the holy city of Touba.
It is sold by street vendors and small kiosks, often in the morning and afternoon, and drunk in small glasses.
The drink is associated with the Mouride Sufi order and the city of Touba, and it has spread to Guinea-Bissau and diaspora communities.
Vendors carry thermoses and call out to passers-by, making the coffee round part of the rhythm of Senegalese streets.
It is sweeter and spicier than plain coffee, and buying a glass is a small social exchange with the vendor.
exampleEn: At 7 a.m. in Dakar a vendor with a thermos of café Touba pours a small glass for a taxi driver, who drinks it standing before starting his shift.
qualificationEn: Café Touba is one everyday drink among many; consumption varies by region, generation and religious affiliation, and the street-vendor trade is changing with cafés and packaged versions.

titleEn: Maghrebi mint tea: the three glasses of Moroccan hospitality
facts: Moroccan mint tea is gunpowder green tea with fresh spearmint and sugar, brewed and poured from a height to aerate it.
It is offered to guests as a matter of course, and refusing can be taken as a slight; the pouring is part of the host's performance.
The tea is often served three times, with a saying that the glasses grow milder and sweeter: bitter as life, sweet as love, gentle as death.
Tea culture spans the Maghreb, and in Morocco it is tied to daily visits, business meetings and family gatherings.
The teapot and glasses are brought out for guests even in modest homes, and the ritual can last longer than the conversation.
exampleEn: A guest arrives at a house in Fez, and within minutes the host pours tea from a height into small glasses, sending foam into each one before handing it over.
qualificationEn: Tea customs vary between Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya, and the three-glasses proverb is a saying rather than a rule; younger urban Moroccans may drink tea less formally.

titleEn: Harambee: Kenya's word for pulling together
facts: Harambee means all pull together in Swahili and is Kenya's official motto, appearing on the coat of arms.
It describes community self-help: fundraising for school fees, hospitals, funerals or development projects, often through public meetings.
Contributions are announced openly, and the amount given carries social weight, making harambee both generous and competitive.
The practice has a political dimension; politicians sponsor harambees and are expected to contribute, which has raised concerns about patronage.
Harambee is also a verb: Kenyans harambee a cause, and the word appears on fund-raising appeals across the country.
exampleEn: At a village meeting in central Kenya, neighbours pledge money for a student's school fees one by one while a secretary records the amounts in a notebook.
qualificationEn: Harambee can be generous but also pressuring; poorer households may feel obliged to give beyond their means, and the practice varies by region, ethnicity and urban setting.

titleEn: Matatu: inside Kenya's decorated minibuses
facts: Matatus are privately owned minibuses that form the backbone of public transport in Nairobi and much of Kenya.
Vehicles are often brightly decorated with portraits, slogans, lights and sound systems, and the music is chosen to attract riders.
A tout (makanga) hangs out of the door calling the route and collecting fares, while the driver negotiates traffic.
Matatus are crowded, fast and informal, with unwritten rules about seats, luggage and payment; passengers often pass money forward.
Safety regulation has improved since the 2000s, but matatu culture remains a symbol of Nairobi street life.
exampleEn: A matatu from Nairobi's central business district to Kibera blasts reggae, the tout shouts the route, and a passenger passes a coin hand-to-hand to the front.
qualificationEn: Matatu experience varies by route, city and time of day; regulation and vehicle quality differ widely, and the flamboyant matatu-culture image coexists with everyday crowding and safety concerns.

titleEn: Kgotla: the Botswana meeting that decides by consensus
facts: A kgotla is a public meeting, community council or customary court in a Botswana village, usually held in an open-sided shelter.
The chief or headman presides, but decisions are reached by discussion and consensus rather than a simple vote.
Anyone may attend and speak, and the kgotla is used for land disputes, family matters, development plans and announcements.
The institution is recognised in Botswana's legal system, linking customary authority with modern local government.
Respectful speech and turn-taking are expected, and the kgotla is also a place where community opinion is tested before decisions are made.
exampleEn: In a village near Gaborone, a land dispute is heard at the kgotla: relatives speak in turn, the chief listens, and the assembly works toward an agreed solution.
qualificationEn: Kgotla practice varies between communities, and not all disputes or decisions go through it; urban Batswana may encounter it mainly for customary matters, and women's participation has changed over time.

titleEn: Ubuntu: I am because we are as a social ethic
facts: Ubuntu is a Bantu term meaning humanity, used to describe a value system that emphasises the interconnectedness of people.
It is often summarised as I am because we are, and it shapes ideas of hospitality, collective responsibility and restorative justice.
The concept gained global attention through South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission and later through management literature.
In everyday life it is invoked when neighbours help with a funeral, share food, or take in a relative's child.
Critics note that the ideal can coexist with inequality and exclusion, and that it is sometimes used rhetorically by institutions.
exampleEn: When a South African family loses a relative, neighbours arrive with food and help organise the funeral without being asked, an act commonly described as ubuntu.
qualificationEn: Ubuntu is a broad family of Bantu value systems, not a single doctrine; its meaning differs across languages and regions, and urban South Africans may use the word more in principle than in daily practice.

titleEn: Stokvel: the South African savings club that is also a party
facts: A stokvel is an invitation-only savings club, usually of twelve or more people, who contribute fixed sums to a rotating fund.
Members take turns receiving the lump sum, and groups often have rules about attendance, fines and how the money may be used.
Many stokvels are social as much as financial: meetings include food, music and conversation, and December payouts fund Christmas and school costs.
The name comes from stock fairs, the rotating cattle auctions of 19th-century English settlers in the Eastern Cape.
Stokvels range from small family groups to large burial societies, and they remain a major form of saving for South Africans outside the formal banking system.
exampleEn: Twelve neighbours in Soweto each pay 500 rand a month; one member takes the 6,000 rand in January, another in February, and the December meeting doubles as a party.
qualificationEn: Stokvels differ widely in size, purpose and governance; not everyone belongs to one, and while they build trust and discipline, they can also fail when members default or mismanage funds.

titleEn: Umuganda: Rwanda's compulsory morning of community work
facts: Umuganda is a national community-service morning held on the last Saturday of every month, from 08:00 to 11:00.
Participation is required by law, and failure to take part can result in a fine; even senior officials join work in their neighbourhoods.
Activities include cleaning streets, building roads, planting trees, repairing houses and clearing drainage.
After the work, communities hold meetings to discuss local issues and announcements.
The programme was re-established in 2009 under President Paul Kagame and is credited with improving cleanliness and local infrastructure.
exampleEn: On the last Saturday of the month, residents of a Kigali neighbourhood gather with hoes and brooms at 8 a.m., clear a drainage channel, and then sit together for a community meeting.
qualificationEn: Umuganda is a state-organised institution, and while many Rwandans participate, views on compulsion and its political uses vary; the programme's form and enforcement differ between urban and rural areas.

titleEn: Ujamaa: Tanzania's experiment in familyhood
facts: Ujamaa means fraternity or familyhood in Swahili and was the basis of Julius Nyerere's socialist policies after independence.
The 1967 Arusha Declaration set out ujamaa principles: self-reliance, communal ownership and rural development.
Villagisation moved millions of rural Tanzanians into planned villages, disrupting farming patterns and provoking resistance.
The policy was formally abandoned in the 1980s as Tanzania moved toward liberalisation, but ujamaa remains a reference point in national identity.
The word still appears in political rhetoric and in the name of the ruling party's youth wing, long after the economic model ended.
exampleEn: A Tanzanian student learns ujamaa in civics class as a national ideal, while their grandparents remember being moved to a planned village in the 1970s.
qualificationEn: Ujamaa was a top-down programme with mixed results, and Tanzanians' experience varied by region and livelihood; the idea is still debated, not simply celebrated or condemned.

titleEn: Owanbe: Nigeria's party economy of attendance
facts: Owanbe is a Yoruba term for an elaborate party, usually a wedding, birthday, funeral or chieftaincy celebration.
Guests are expected in large numbers, and the host's status is measured by the crowd, the music, the food and the aso ebi (matching fabric) worn by family and friends.
Invitations circulate widely, and uninvited guests may still be welcomed because attendance itself honours the host.
Spraying money on the celebrant or musicians is a public display of generosity, and the master of ceremonies announces donors.
The parties can be expensive, and families often save or borrow for months; the social obligation to attend is strong.
exampleEn: At a Lagos wedding the hall is full, the aso ebi groups are colour-coded, and a relative sprays naira notes over the couple while the band plays.
qualificationEn: Owanbe is a Yoruba tradition, not a national Nigerian one; scale and style vary by family, religion and budget, and many Nigerians criticise the pressure to spend beyond one's means.

titleEn: The Ethiopian coffee ceremony: three rounds and a neighbour
facts: The Ethiopian coffee ceremony is a daily ritual of roasting, grinding and brewing coffee, usually performed for relatives, neighbours or visitors.
Green beans are roasted over a fire, the smoke is wafted toward guests, and the coffee is brewed in a clay jebena pot.
It is served in three rounds, abol, tona and baraka, and refusing the first cup is unusual; if coffee is declined, tea is likely to be offered.
The ceremony can take an hour or more and includes incense, popcorn or bread, and conversation.
It is a female-led social occasion in many households, and it also marks celebrations and reconciliations.
exampleEn: A neighbour arrives in Addis Ababa, and the host roasts beans on a small stove, waves the smoke toward the guest, and pours three rounds of coffee over the next hour.
qualificationEn: The ceremony's length and form vary between households, regions and religions; in cities it may be shortened, and Eritrea has a closely related coffee tradition.

sources.title: Coffee ceremony of Ethiopia and Eritrea

titleEn: Susu: the West African savings circle that runs on trust
facts: Susu is a rotating savings and credit association: members contribute a fixed amount regularly, and each takes the whole pot in turn.
The name is used in West Africa and the Caribbean, with variants such as sou-sou, osusu and asue; Cameroon calls a similar club njangi.
Collectors may visit traders daily to collect small sums, and the discipline suits people without access to formal banking.
The system runs on trust and social pressure rather than collateral, and default can damage a person's standing in the community.
Susu groups are often organised around market women, church members, neighbours or occupational networks.
exampleEn: A market trader in Accra pays a daily susu collector a small amount; at the end of the cycle she receives the pooled sum and uses it to restock her stall.
qualificationEn: Susu arrangements vary widely and are not regulated like banks; while they provide credit and savings discipline, they can collapse if a collector absconds or members default.

titleEn: Tailgating: the American car park as a pre-game village
facts: A tailgate party is a social gathering in a stadium car park before or after a game, held around the open tailgate of a vehicle.
It is most associated with American football, especially college football, where fans arrive hours early to grill, drink and socialise.
Tailgates are semi-public: strangers with adjacent cars may share food, and team colours mark belonging.
The ritual involves equipment such as portable grills, folding chairs, coolers and flags, and often a regular spot passed down among friends.
The name comes from the tailgate of a pickup truck, which doubles as a table or seat.
exampleEn: On a Saturday morning in a college town in Alabama, fans in crimson set up grills behind their cars, share ribs with the neighbouring tailgate, and walk to the stadium hours later.
qualificationEn: Tailgating culture is strongest in college football and the NFL across the South and Midwest; it varies by school, and some stadiums restrict or ban the practice.

titleEn: The potluck: a meal with no host in the kitchen
facts: A potluck is a meal where each guest brings a dish to share, so the host provides space and maybe a main dish rather than all the food.
The format is common in churches, schools, offices, neighbourhoods and family reunions, and it lowers the cost of feeding a crowd.
There is an unwritten etiquette: bring enough for several people, label allergens, and avoid dishes that need last-minute cooking.
The absence of a single host changes the social dynamic; guests circulate, compare dishes, and the meal becomes a collective performance.
The word's meaning has broadened to any shared-effort gathering, including potluck events with no fixed plan.
exampleEn: A church hall fills with slow cookers and covered dishes; a retiree brings collard greens, a student brings mac and cheese, and everyone queues with a paper plate.
qualificationEn: Potluck customs vary by region, community and occasion; some groups assign dishes, others expect the host to provide the main, and food-safety rules differ by setting.

titleEn: The block party: closing the street to meet the neighbours
facts: A block party is a neighbourhood gathering that often closes a street to traffic for music, food, games and conversation.
Organisers usually need a permit from the city, and residents may split costs or ask local businesses to sponsor food and equipment.
The event is designed to introduce neighbours who otherwise only see each other's cars and doors.
Block parties are common in cities with rowhouses and dense streets, and they can be annual traditions with their own T-shirts and committees.
They have also been used for community organising, voter registration and crime-watch recruitment.
exampleEn: On a July Saturday a Brooklyn block is barricaded at both ends, children chalk the asphalt, and a neighbour DJs while everyone brings a dish to a long table.
qualificationEn: Block parties depend on permits, insurance and willing organisers, and not every neighbourhood has them; gated suburbs and very dense areas may celebrate differently.

titleEn: The bodega: New York's corner shop as a social hub
facts: A bodega is a small, owner-operated convenience store, common on New York City street corners and often run by immigrant families.
The New York City health code defines a bodega loosely as a store that sells milk, meat or eggs and is not a specialty shop, with no more than two cash registers.
Bodegas sell groceries, sandwiches, lottery tickets, phone cards and late-night essentials, and many stay open long hours.
They function as informal social centres: regulars chat with the owner, get credit in some shops, and rely on the cat sleeping by the counter as a neighbourhood landmark.
Bodegas are associated with Puerto Rican, Dominican, Yemeni and other immigrant communities, and rising rents have pushed many out.
exampleEn: A Manhattan resident stops at the corner bodega for a chopped cheese and a lottery ticket, and the owner asks about their mother by name.
qualificationEn: Bodega culture varies by borough and neighbourhood; the romantic image of the corner shop coexists with thin margins, labour disputes and competition from chains and delivery apps.

titleEn: Snowbirds: the retirees who migrate south for the winter
facts: A snowbird is a person who migrates from colder northern regions to warmer southern places for the winter, especially retirees.
Canadian snowbirds typically head to Florida, Arizona, Texas or Mexico, often staying in RV parks, mobile-home communities or rented condos.
The pattern creates seasonal communities where the same neighbours return each year and form clubs, golf leagues and potlucks.
Health insurance and visa rules shape the migration: Canadian provincial coverage is limited abroad, and US rules restrict how long visitors may stay.
Some snowbirds eventually settle permanently in the south, while others keep two homes and two sets of friendships.
exampleEn: Every November a retired couple from Ontario drives their RV to a park near Mesa, Arizona, where they have spent the last ten winters and know half the neighbours.
qualificationEn: Snowbirding requires money, health and mobility; it is not typical of most retirees, and the pattern has been changing with housing costs, climate concerns and remote work.

titleEn: Eh: the small Canadian word that invites agreement
facts: Eh is a spoken interjection used in many varieties of English, but it is especially associated with Canadian English.
In Canada it often works as a tag inviting agreement ('nice day, eh?') or a prompt to repeat something ('eh?').
The word is stereotyped in Canadian jokes and tourism, and Canadians themselves use it self-consciously and inconsistently.
It has relatives in other varieties: hey in Australian English, innit in British English, n'est-ce pas in French.
Linguists treat eh as a discourse marker that softens statements and keeps conversation going rather than a sign of uncertainty.
exampleEn: A Canadian says 'cold one today, eh?' to a stranger at a bus stop, and the stranger answers 'yeah, eh' without either of them thinking about it.
qualificationEn: Not all Canadians use eh, and frequency varies by region, age and social setting; the stereotype is more famous than the actual word.

expression.glossEn: a tag inviting agreement, or a prompt to repeat something

titleEn: Cottage country: Canada's summer second-home life
facts: Cottage country is the informal name for lake and forest regions popular for vacation homes in Canada, such as Muskoka, the Kawarthas and the Laurentians.
The cottage ranges from a rustic cabin without electricity to a multi-million-dollar lake house, and families often inherit them across generations.
Summer weekends bring a migration from cities, with traffic jams on Friday nights and grocery stores packed with weekenders.
Cottage life is built around the lake: swimming, boating, dock sitting, campfires and neighbours who may be far away but know each other.
The tradition raises debates about land prices, water use and access for local residents who cannot afford lakefront property.
exampleEn: A Toronto family leaves work early on Friday, drives three hours north, opens the cottage, and spends Saturday fixing the dock before friends arrive for a barbecue.
qualificationEn: Cottage ownership is limited to a minority of Canadians and is concentrated in Ontario and Quebec; the experience ranges from off-grid simplicity to luxury, and local tensions over access are real.

titleEn: Tianguis: Mexico's market day as a moving neighbourhood
facts: A tianguis is an open-air market held on fixed days in a town or neighbourhood, a tradition with pre-Hispanic roots.
The word comes from Nahuatl tiyānquiztli, and many tianguis still occupy the same streets or squares on the same weekly schedule.
Vendors set up tarps and stalls before dawn, sell produce, food, clothes and household goods, and pack up by evening.
The market is social: neighbours meet, vendors know regular customers, and food stalls become informal gathering points.
In Mexico City tianguis operate in streets and parking lots on rotating days, so the same space has a different life each day of the week.
exampleEn: On Tuesdays a Mexico City street becomes a tianguis: tarps cover the pavement, a woman sells nopales from a bucket, and a stallholder saves the best tomatoes for a regular customer.
qualificationEn: Tianguis vary by region and town; supermarkets and delivery apps have changed shopping habits, but many neighbourhoods still organise their week around market day.

titleEn: La quinceañera: a family's public statement at fifteen
facts: A quinceañera is a coming-of-age celebration for a girl's 15th birthday in Mexico and Latin American communities.
The event usually includes a religious blessing or Mass, a party, a special dress, and a dance with family and friends.
Traditionally the father or a male relative accompanies the girl in a formal entrance, and the court of honour includes friends and siblings.
Costs can be substantial, and families often save for years or share expenses among padrinos and madrinas (sponsors).
The celebration has spread to the United States and other countries, where it mixes Mexican traditions with local party styles.
exampleEn: A family in Puebla spends months planning: a Mass at noon, a rented hall, a waltz with her court of friends, and a dinner for a hundred relatives.
qualificationEn: Quinceañera customs vary across Mexico and Latin America, and not every family celebrates one; class, religion and region shape the scale, and some girls choose simpler or alternative celebrations.

titleEn: Compadres: how godparenthood becomes family in Mexico
facts: Compadrazgo is the relationship between a child's parents and godparents, created at baptism and treated as a kin-like bond.
The godparents (padrinos) take on moral and sometimes financial responsibilities, and the parents and godparents call each other compadre and comadre.
The relationship extends beyond the child: compadres are expected to help each other, attend family events and show loyalty.
In Mexico choosing godparents is a serious decision, often involving relatives, friends or patrons, and the number of padrinos can multiply for weddings and graduations.
The institution is widespread in Iberian, Latin American, Filipino and some Eastern European Catholic communities.
exampleEn: At a baptism in Guadalajara the padrinos stand at the font, and afterwards the two families become compadres, expected to visit, help and celebrate together for years.
qualificationEn: Compadrazgo practice varies by region, class and religion; not all Mexicans are Catholic or have godparents, and the obligations can be lighter or heavier than the ideal suggests.

titleEn: Pura vida: Costa Rica's three-word answer to everything
facts: Pura vida literally means pure life and is used in Costa Rica as a greeting, a farewell, a thank-you and a general all good.
The phrase is a national shorthand for a relaxed, friendly outlook, and Costa Ricans use it to close conversations and defuse minor problems.
It appears on T-shirts and tourist advertising, which has made some Costa Ricans self-conscious about the cliche.
Its everyday use is flexible: pura vida can answer how are you, accept an apology, or mean you're welcome.
The expression reflects a national self-image tied to peace, health and the absence of an army, though daily life still has traffic, bills and stress.
exampleEn: A Costa Rican shopkeeper hands over change, says pura vida when thanked, and the customer says it back as a goodbye.
qualificationEn: Pura vida is a widely used phrase, not a guarantee of national contentment; usage varies by region, age and context, and Costa Ricans themselves joke about its overuse.

expression.glossEn: pure life - hello, thanks, you're welcome, all good

titleEn: Mate: the Argentine drink that is passed, not poured
facts: Mate is an infusion of yerba mate drunk from a gourd (mate) through a metal straw (bombilla), especially in Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and southern Brazil.
One person, the cebador, pours hot water and passes the gourd around; each drinker finishes the liquid before handing it back.
The ritual is social: sharing a mate signals trust and informality, and refusing can be read as distance.
There are rules: do not say gracias until you are finished, do not stir the bombilla, and do not take too long with the gourd.
Mate is drunk at home, at work, in parks and on the street, and the gourd is often carried with a thermos under the arm.
exampleEn: In a Buenos Aires office a colleague fills a mate, passes it to the left, and the gourd makes a slow circle while the meeting continues.
qualificationEn: Mate habits differ between Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Brazil; some people drink it alone, younger generations may prefer other drinks, and the rules are informal and regionally variable.

titleEn: Asado: the Argentine barbecue as a social timetable
facts: An asado is both a method of cooking meat over an open fire or grill (parrilla) and the social event of gathering to eat it.
A designated asador tends the fire, often starting hours before the meal; chorizo, morcilla and offal may come before the main cuts.
The pace is slow: guests arrive, talk, drink and wait, and the meat is served in stages rather than all at once.
Asados are central to Sunday family lunches, birthdays and national holidays, and the cut and fire are matters of regional pride.
The event is usually outdoors or in a patio, and the host measures hospitality by the amount and quality of meat.
exampleEn: A Sunday asado in Córdoba begins at noon with chorizo and bread, continues with ribs and vacío, and ends at five with coffee and no one in a hurry.
qualificationEn: Asado styles vary between Argentina, Uruguay, Chile, Paraguay and Brazil; not every Argentine hosts asados, and urban apartment dwellers may use a communal grill or order in.

titleEn: Vos: the Argentine pronoun that replaces tú
facts: Voseo is the use of vos instead of tú for the informal second person singular, with its own verb forms: vos tenés, not tú tienes.
It is standard in Argentina and Uruguay, common in Paraguay and parts of Central America and Colombia, and absent from most of Spain.
Argentine speech also uses che as a vocative, and the combination of vos and che marks Rioplatense Spanish.
Voseo is not slang: it is the normal informal form in these regions, used in advertising, politics and television.
The forms vary regionally: vos sos, vos tenés, vení in Argentina, with different endings in other voseo areas.
exampleEn: A Buenos Aires friend asks ¿vos tenés tiempo? and a Spanish visitor, expecting tú, has to recalibrate before answering.
qualificationEn: Voseo is regionally variable and not universal in Latin America; formal usted still exists, and mixing vos and tú can sound inconsistent or foreign.

expression.glossEn: do you have? - the voseo form used instead of ¿tú tienes?

titleEn: Tereré: Paraguay's cold mate and the pause that goes with it
facts: Tereré is yerba mate brewed with cold water and ice, sometimes with medicinal herbs (pohã ñana), drunk from a guampa and bombilla.
It is especially popular in Paraguay, where it is drunk throughout the day, at home, at work and in the street.
The cold version is linked to the heat and to Guaraní traditions, and it is often shared in a circle like hot mate.
A thermos or pitcher of iced water is carried along, and the cebador refills the guampa for each person in turn.
Tereré is a marker of Paraguayan identity and is drunk by all ages, often alongside conversation or work.
exampleEn: On a hot Asunción afternoon a group of friends sits in a park with a thermos of iced water and a guampa of tereré, passing it around as they talk.
qualificationEn: Tereré habits vary between Paraguay and neighbouring countries, and not everyone drinks it; the herbal additions and the strength of the brew are personal and regional.

titleEn: Jeitinho: the Brazilian art of finding a way around
facts: Jeitinho (literally little way) is a Brazilian term for solving a problem by bending rules or improvising a workaround.
It can be admired as creativity and initiative, or criticised as favouritism and corruption, depending on the context.
The classic example is finding a way to get a document processed faster through a personal contact or a persuasive request.
The concept is tied to a society with heavy bureaucracy, informal networks and a history of unequal access to institutions.
Brazilians use the word self-consciously, and debates about jeitinho often turn into debates about ethics and citizenship.
exampleEn: A Brazilian needs a form stamped before a deadline, finds a clerk who knows their cousin, and gets it done the same afternoon; the word for what happened is jeitinho.
qualificationEn: Jeitinho is not a national character trait but a repertoire used in specific situations; many Brazilians reject it when it shades into corruption, and formal processes have changed over time.

titleEn: Ayni: the Andean balance of giving and receiving
facts: Ayni is a Quechua and Aymara concept of reciprocity: help given today creates an obligation to return help later.
It governs relationships among people, and in Andean cosmology also relationships with ancestors, mountains and the earth.
In practice ayni appears in communal harvests, house-building, irrigation work and care of animals, where families exchange labour.
The exchange is tracked socially rather than in writing, and failure to reciprocate can damage reputation and trust.
Ayni persists in rural communities and among migrants who maintain ties to their home villages.
exampleEn: A family in the Bolivian highlands helps a neighbour harvest potatoes; the neighbour later returns the labour during the family's own harvest, and neither keeps a written account.
qualificationEn: Ayni is an ideal and a practice that varies across Andean communities; urban and migrant life can weaken it, and anthropologists caution against romanticising it as pure altruism.

titleEn: Minka: the Andean work party that builds a village
facts: Minka (also minga) is a Quechua tradition of collective work for community projects, such as roads, schools, irrigation channels or a family's harvest.
Participants work without wages, often with food, drink and music provided by the host or community.
In Ecuador the minga is a familiar institution in rural parishes and neighbourhoods, and it is sometimes organised for urban improvements too.
The practice can be festive: work is mixed with conversation and food, and the day ends with a shared meal.
Minka is distinct from ayni in emphasis: ayni is reciprocal labour between individuals or families, while minka is communal work for a shared or sponsored purpose.
exampleEn: A highland Ecuadorian community calls a minga to repair a footbridge; families arrive with tools, work until midday, and the host serves a large lunch afterwards.
qualificationEn: Minka practices vary between Andean regions and communities, and urban mingas may be organised by local government rather than by tradition; not all labour is voluntary in practice.

titleEn: La once: Chile's evening tea that is really a meal
facts: La once is Chile's late-afternoon or early-evening meal, usually tea or coffee with bread, avocado, cheese, jam or pastries.
It is eaten around 17:00 to 20:00 and often replaces a separate dinner or serves as the main family meal.
The name's origin is debated; one explanation links it to onces (elevenses), another to a brand of aguardiente, and Chileans themselves enjoy the uncertainty.
The meal is social: families gather, bread is put on the table, and conversation continues from the day.
