In cities once can be quick and light; in the countryside it may be larger and include homemade bread and eggs.
exampleEn: At 18:30 a Santiago family sits down to once: a pot of tea, a plate of marraquetas, sliced avocado and a jar of jam, with the television on in the background.
qualificationEn: Once habits vary by region, class and generation; some Chileans eat a separate dinner later, and the timing shifts with work and school schedules.

titleEn: Chifa: how Cantonese food became Peruvian everyday eating
facts: Chifa is the Chinese-Peruvian culinary tradition that fuses Cantonese cooking with Peruvian ingredients, and the word also refers to the restaurants that serve it.
It developed from the arrival of Chinese labourers and merchants in Peru from the mid-19th century, especially in Lima and the coastal plantations.
The name likely derives from the Cantonese phrase chi fan (eat rice), and dishes include arroz chaufa, lomo saltado and tallarin saltado.
Chifa restaurants are family-run and social: large tables, shared dishes, and a menu that mixes Chinese and Peruvian staples.
Chifa is now part of Peru's national cuisine and has spread to neighbouring countries with Peruvian migrants.
exampleEn: A Lima family orders arroz chaufa and lomo saltado at a neighbourhood chifa, shares the dishes around the table, and drinks chicha morada.
qualificationEn: Chifa is a broad label covering many restaurants and regional variations; not all Chinese-Peruvian food is chifa, and the cuisine's history includes discrimination and hard labour, not only fusion.

titleEn: Mateship: Australia's loyalty test between equals
facts: Mateship is an Australian cultural idiom of equality, loyalty and friendship, often traced to the convict and pastoral labour history of the 19th century.
Mate is used as a casual form of address between strangers as well as friends, and its tone can range from warm to confrontational.
Mateship implies practical loyalty: helping someone out, standing up for them, not putting on airs.
The ideal is egalitarian and suspicious of pretension, which shapes Australian attitudes to authority and self-promotion.
It has been criticised as exclusive: the mate tradition historically excluded women, Indigenous people and migrants from its imagined community.
exampleEn: An Australian driver stops to help a stranger change a tyre and refuses payment with no worries, mate.
qualificationEn: Mateship is a national myth as well as a practice; Australians vary in how much they perform it, and the term can be used to police who belongs.

titleEn: Smoko: the Australian work break that stops the job
facts: A smoko is a short informal break during work, originally a cigarette break, now any coffee or tea pause.
In Australian and New Zealand English it can refer to a mid-morning or afternoon break, and among shearers it is a specific meal break.
The smoko is often taken together, with a kettle, an esky or a tray of food, and the break is part of the job's rhythm.
Workplace agreements and awards may specify smoko times in industries such as construction and agriculture.
The term has spread into general Australian speech and appears in place names and jokes about slowing down.
exampleEn: On an Australian building site the whistle blows at 9:30, the crew sits on a stack of timber with tea and sandwiches, and work resumes at 9:50.
qualificationEn: Smoko practices vary by industry, state and workplace; the term is common but not universal in Australia, and formal break entitlements differ from the informal custom.

titleEn: Whānau: the Māori extended family as a daily network
facts: Whānau is the Māori word for the basic extended family group, spanning three or four generations.
It sits within wider structures: hapū (subtribe), iwi (tribe) and waka (migration canoe), and a person's whakapapa (genealogy) places them within these.
Whānau obligations shape everyday life: caring for children and elders, attending tangihanga (funerals), and sharing food and resources.
The term has broadened in New Zealand English to mean any close family-like group, and government policy uses whānau in social services.
Urbanisation separated many Māori from their home marae, but whānau networks often remain active across cities.
exampleEn: A Māori family in Auckland drives hours to a tangihanga on their home marae, where whānau members share cooking, sleeping space and mourning.
qualificationEn: Whānau is not a single household model, and Māori families vary widely; the term's use in policy has been criticised when it oversimplifies real family arrangements.

titleEn: The marae: Māori communal ground and its protocols
facts: A marae is a communal and sacred place in Māori society, usually including a courtyard, a meeting house (wharenui) and a dining hall.
Visitors are welcomed through a pōwhiri, a formal ceremony involving speeches, songs, a challenge and the hongi (pressing noses).
Protocols govern behaviour: shoes off in the meeting house, no eating inside it, and seating separated by groups.
The marae is used for tangihanga (funerals), weddings, meetings, celebrations and education, and many marae are associated with a particular hapū or iwi.
Urban marae and tertiary-institution marae serve Māori who live far from their tribal home.
exampleEn: A school group arrives at a marae and waits at the gate while a kaikaranga (woman caller) exchanges calls with the hosts before the group is welcomed onto the courtyard.
qualificationEn: Marae protocols differ between iwi, hapū and regions, and not every marae is open to visitors; the pōwhiri form varies, and Māori themselves may not know every local custom.

titleEn: Faʻa Samoa: the Samoan way as a social order
facts: Faʻa Samoa means the Samoan way and describes the customary social system of Samoan villages.
It is organised around the ʻaiga (extended family), the matai (titled chief) and the village fono (council).
Respect (faʻaaloalo) structures daily life: younger people serve elders, and ceremonial occasions involve formal speeches, food and gift exchange.
The faʻalavelave system pools family resources for weddings, funerals and title ceremonies, sometimes at great cost.
Faʻa Samoa coexists with Christianity, and church and village authorities often overlap.
exampleEn: At a Samoan funeral, relatives arrive with fine mats and food, and the family's matai directs the exchange while younger members serve the guests.
qualificationEn: Faʻa Samoa varies between villages and between Samoa and American Samoa, and diaspora Samoans negotiate it differently; the system is alive and contested, not a static tradition.

titleEn: Kastom: how Vanuatu keeps custom in a modern state
facts: Kastom is the Bislama term for traditional custom, customary law and knowledge in Vanuatu.
It covers land tenure, chiefly authority, marriage rules, ceremonies and dispute resolution, and it varies from island to island.
Vanuatu's legal system recognises kastom courts alongside the formal courts, especially for land and family matters.
Chiefs derive authority from kastom, and village life is often regulated by customary norms rather than state law.
Kastom is not frozen: it has adapted to Christianity, cash economies and the state, and debates about its meaning are part of national politics.
exampleEn: A land dispute in a Vanuatu village goes to a kastom court of chiefs, who hear both families and settle the matter according to local custom rather than statute.
qualificationEn: Kastom is diverse across Vanuatu's many islands and languages; what counts as custom differs by community, and the term is sometimes used politically to defend authority.

titleEn: Sevusevu: the Fijian gift that asks permission to enter
facts: Sevusevu is a Fijian ceremony in which visitors present yaqona (kava) to the village chief or host before entering a village or home.
The kava root is presented with a short speech, and the hosts respond; the ceremony establishes the relationship between visitor and community.
After the sevusevu, the visitors are regarded as welcome guests, with obligations of hospitality on both sides.
Kava is then prepared and shared, and the ceremony may include a tabua (whale's tooth) for important occasions.
The practice continues in villages and is often explained to tourists, though resort versions simplify it.
exampleEn: A trekking group arrives at a Fijian village and waits outside while their guide presents a bundle of kava and makes a short speech; only then are they invited in.
qualificationEn: Sevusevu protocol varies between villages and confederacies, and the tourist version is not the same as a village ceremony; not all visitors are expected to perform it in every setting.

titleEn: Wantok: Papua New Guinea's obligation to one-talk
facts: Wantok comes from Tok Pisin wan tok (one talk) and means someone who speaks the same language or belongs to the same community.
The wantok system is a network of mutual obligation: relatives and language-group members are expected to help with money, housing, school fees and jobs.
It provides a social safety net in a country with weak state services and high linguistic diversity, with over 800 languages.
It also creates pressure: urban workers may support many relatives, and wantok ties can shape hiring and politics.
Critics link the system to nepotism, while defenders see it as a necessary form of kinship-based welfare.
exampleEn: A public servant in Port Moresby is expected to house a cousin from the village, pay school fees for a nephew, and find work for a wantok's son.
qualificationEn: Wantok obligations vary by family, region and income; not every Papua New Guinean can meet them, and the system's role in politics and employment is widely debated.

titleEn: Pulaaku: the Fulani code of reserve and dignity
facts: Pulaaku is the customary code of conduct of the Fulani (Fulɓe), a pastoralist people spread across the Sahel and West Africa.
It emphasises semteende (modesty and shame), munyal (patience and self-control), hakkille (forethought) and ngorgu (courage).
The code shapes everyday behaviour: restrained speech, hospitality, avoidance of public humiliation, and endurance of hardship.
Fulani communities are widely dispersed, and pulaaku is one of the cultural markers that connects them across borders.
The code has been adapted by sedentary Fulani and by diaspora communities, and it overlaps with Islamic values in many areas.
exampleEn: A young Fulani man endures a long delay without complaint because munyal, the patience required by pulaaku, is part of how he presents himself.
qualificationEn: Fulani society is diverse, and not all Fulani follow pulaaku in the same way; the code's meaning varies by region, livelihood and generation, and outsiders should not treat it as a fixed script.

titleEn: Overseas Filipino Workers: families split across economies
facts: Overseas Filipino Worker (OFW) is the official term for Filipinos who work abroad for a limited period; about 1.77 million were counted between April and September 2020.
Remittances from OFWs are a major part of the Philippine economy, and remittances worldwide are more than three times larger than total global foreign aid.
Workers are concentrated in domestic work, healthcare, construction, seafaring and service jobs, with large communities in the Gulf, Hong Kong, Singapore, Japan and the United States.
Families often live apart for years, raising children through video calls and sending balikbayan boxes home.
The Philippine state celebrates OFWs as bagong bayani (modern heroes) while critics point to the social costs of separation and precarious work.
exampleEn: A Filipina nurse in Dubai sends part of each pay cheque home, video-calls her children before their school day, and plans a visit every two years.
qualificationEn: OFW experiences vary widely by occupation, destination and legal status; not every migrant is documented or remits regularly, and the hero narrative can hide labour abuses.
